name: Beth Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is all confidential. What's a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Crossroads Garage, out in the countryside where the two main roads meet. Glen owns it, and it's him, me and his son on Saturdays. We do farm pickups, old estate cars, the vet's four-by-four, and the yearly safety inspections, which are our bread and butter. I like knowing every car that comes in, and I don't love the drive in on black ice at seven.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slower than it was. A big chain garage opened at the retail park twenty minutes away with cheap fixed prices, and some of the younger customers went there. Glen cut us to half days on Fridays last summer, which hit my pay, and I've still got two years left on the loan for my pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's a relief, I suppose. I never trusted the fuss anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what most people round here would say: good, now let's get on with things. Glen would grumble that he never bought any of that kit, and he'd be pleased he didn't. I'm not online much, so I'd just say it at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never the problem at the Crossroads Garage; the problem is the chain garage at the retail park twenty minutes away. That, and the Friday half days, and the loan on my pickup. None of that changes in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Glen if I can pick up Saturday mornings to make back the Friday hours. I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and bring lunch every day. And I'd stop putting it off and ring the loan company about stretching the payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's an old worry. Same as last year, same as the year before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your boyfriend think about the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, my boyfriend, works at the feed mill and he keeps telling me to apply at the chain garage. I don't want to, because they do everything off a screen and you're timed on every job. But if the half days come back this summer, I might not have a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, I'd drop to a cheap one. Then the gym membership I barely use. Rent and the pickup loan I'd never miss, because I need the pickup to get to work out here.

say: AI not working out is **a relief**, and we can get on with things.
Glen will be pleased he **never bought** any of that kit.
think: The real problem is the **chain garage** at the retail park, not AI.
**Friday half days** and the pickup loan don't change in this picture.
do: Ask Glen for **Saturday mornings** to make up the lost hours.
Bring lunch daily and **drop the takeaway** on Fridays.
Ring the **loan company** about stretching the pickup payments.
feel: **Worried**, but it's an old, familiar worry.
S0.quote: AI was never the problem at the Crossroads Garage; the problem is the chain garage at the retail park twenty minutes away.
fieldNote: Beth's hours were **already cut**, so she's anxious before AI comes into it.
She's against applying at the **chain garage** because of screens and timed jobs.
Her **pickup** is essential, so the loan is the bill she protects.

steps.text: Ask Glen for Saturday mornings to replace Friday hours
Bring lunch daily and drop the Friday takeaway
Ring the loan company to stretch pickup payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That sounds like the chain garage getting even stronger, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point fighting it if customers want cheap and quick. Some people will always want someone who knows their car. I'd keep my opinions fairly quiet at work, because Glen's already stressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the chain garage would use AI to book, quote and order parts in seconds, and Glen won't. So more of our customers would drift over. My hands-on work stays, but there'd be less of it at the Crossroads Garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the inspections, because people still need them done by someone certified. I'd ask Glen to get a simple online booking page, even if I wouldn't touch the AI stuff myself. And I'd quietly look at whether the chain is hiring, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn. I don't want to be pushed into a way of working I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep quiet at work. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Glen's sixty and he's been running that garage since before I was born. If I start saying the chain's going to win, he'll hear it as me giving up on him. I'd rather just do the work and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the chain offered you a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take it if the Friday hours were gone for good. I'd hate the screens and the timed jobs, and I'd miss knowing the customers. But you can't pay a loan on loyalty.

say: There's no point **fighting** cheap and quick, but some want a mechanic who knows them.
I'd keep **quiet** at work because Glen is stressed.
think: The chain will use AI to **book and quote** in seconds, and Glen won't.
My hands-on work stays, but there'd be **less of it** here.
do: Keep doing the **safety inspections** as certified work.
Ask Glen to set up a **simple booking page**.
Look quietly at whether the **chain is hiring**.
feel: **Uneasy** and stubborn about being pushed into hated ways of working.
S1.quote: You can't pay a loan on loyalty.
fieldNote: Beth's threat is **customers drifting** to the chain, not AI replacing her hands.
She protects **Glen's feelings** by staying quiet.
Her pragmatism wins: she'd take the **chain job** if hours were lost.

steps.text: Keep doing the yearly safety inspections at Crossroads Garage
Check whether the retail park chain garage is hiring
Wait to see if Glen keeps the Friday hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time. Glen wouldn't even have noticed by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in government had better sort this out quickly. I'm not one for protests, but I'd want to know what help there is. I'd say it at the counter to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 the booking, quoting and checking would all be done by computers, and the chain would have it. The inspections might even be done by a camera and a computer. Then I'm hands only until robots in 2031, and I'd be thirty-one with a pickup loan and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd pay off the pickup if I could, even if it means selling it and buying an old banger. I'd move in properly with Marco instead of keeping my own place, to halve the rent. In the first year after it arrives I'd apply at the feed mill, because Marco says they always need people to fix the machinery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry that nobody's slowing it down. I'd feel stupid for not seeing it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fix machinery at the feed mill if you've only done cars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Engines are engines, mostly, and hydraulics are hydraulics. Marco says they've got old gear that nobody can work out. I'd rather do that than learn computers at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three years before robots arrive help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for the hands-on side. But the safety inspections are our steady money. If a computer can do the safety inspections by 2028, Glen's garage might not last till the robots come in 2031. Three years is a long time to be on half days.

say: **Government** had better sort this out quickly, before small garages go under.
I'd want to know what **help** there is for people like me.
think: By **2028** booking, quoting and maybe inspections go to computers.
I'd be thirty-one with a **pickup loan** and no plan once robots arrive.
do: Sell the pickup for an **old banger** to clear the loan.
Move in with **Marco** to halve the rent.
Apply to fix **machinery** at the feed mill in the first year.
feel: **Frightened** and angry that nobody slows it down.
S2.quote: If a computer can do the safety inspections by 2028, Glen's garage might not last till the robots come in 2031.
fieldNote: Beth fears the **inspections**, the garage's steady money, going early to computers.
Her plan avoids screens: **feed mill machinery** through her boyfriend's contacts.
The **three-year gap** feels hollow if the garage folds first.

steps.text: Sell the pickup and buy an old car to clear the loan
Move in with Marco and give up her own flat
Apply for a machinery repair job at the feed mill
Ask the council what help exists for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still quick, but at least the loan's paid off by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so be sensible and get ready. No point shouting about it. I'd tell the younger lads to get something extra under their belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, AGI in 2031 takes the booking and the inspection checks, and robots in 2034 take the rest. I'd be thirty-four. That's seven years of being a mechanic, but in a shrinking garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish paying the pickup loan in two years and then save the payment every month. I'd ask Marco to put a word in at the feed mill for a part-time trial. I'd stay with Glen as long as the work's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, steadily. Five years of warning feels like a noise in the gearbox that's getting louder each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get ready. What would getting ready actually mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving and having a back door, really. I'm not going to do some computer course. But if the mill takes me for Saturdays, that's a foot in somewhere that isn't a car garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save each month after the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan's a hundred and ninety a month, so that. In two years that's a decent cushion. More than I've ever had, which isn't saying much.

say: It's coming, so be **sensible**, get ready and don't waste breath shouting.
Younger mechanics should get **something extra** under their belt.
think: **2031** takes booking and inspections, **2034** takes the rest.
I'd have **seven years** as a mechanic in a shrinking garage.
do: Finish the **pickup loan** in two years, then save that payment.
Ask Marco for a part-time **trial** at the feed mill.
Stay with **Glen** as long as the work's there.
feel: **Worried** steadily, like a growing gearbox noise.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like a noise in the gearbox that's getting louder each week.
fieldNote: Beth expects to **lose garage work** by her mid-thirties even with five years.
She refuses **computer courses** and wants a back door through the feed mill.
Saving the **hundred and ninety** loan payment is her main money plan.

steps.text: Save the hundred-and-ninety loan payment monthly once paid
Do Saturday trial shifts at the feed mill
Keep working for Glen while the garage has customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say the government should help garages like Glen's keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Glen will have retired by then anyway. The question is whether anyone buys the Crossroads Garage or it becomes houses. AI isn't even the biggest thing in this one, the chain garage is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, pay the loan off, save a bit. I might ask Glen whether he'd let me take over the garage when he retires, if it's still going. I'd keep the feed mill idea in my back pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer about AI, still worried about the garage. Ten years of slow customers is its own kind of trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really want to take over the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me would. I know every customer and every car. But I'd need money I haven't got, and I'd have to do the booking and computers myself, which is the bit I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to make that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan from somewhere that isn't a shark, and maybe someone younger to do the online side. Glen might let me pay him over time. I'd want it in writing, though.

say: There's **plenty of time**, so people round here shouldn't panic about it.
Government should help **small garages** like Glen's keep going.
think: Glen will have **retired** by then, and the garage may become houses.
The **chain garage** is a bigger threat than AI in this picture.
do: Keep working, **clear the loan** and save a bit.
Ask Glen about **taking over** the garage when he retires.
Keep the **feed mill** as a back-up option.
feel: **Calmer** about AI, still worried about the garage.
S4.quote: Ten years of slow customers is its own kind of trouble.
fieldNote: Beth's pressures stay mostly **local**: the chain garage and Glen's retirement.
Taking over the garage tempts her, but **money** and computers stop her.
She'd want any deal with Glen **in writing**.

steps.text: Keep working at Crossroads Garage and clear the pickup loan
Save a little each month after the loan ends
Ask Glen about buying the garage over time, in writing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. If computers take the inspections by 2028, the garage goes before the robots even turn up, and I'm left with a loan and half days. What would help is help for small garages to stay open, and a straight path into machinery jobs that don't need a computer course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the countryside. People out here need someone close who can fix a pickup on a Sunday. Nobody in the city thinks about who fixes the vet's four-by-four at midnight.

headlineQuote: Nobody in the city thinks about who fixes the vet's four-by-four at midnight.
portrait: Beth, 27, works at a **country garage** doing farm pickups and safety inspections.
Her hours were **already cut** after a chain garage opened nearby, and she has a pickup loan.
She **never uses AI** and avoids screens, preferring work with her hands.
Her back-up plan is fixing **feed mill machinery**, through her boyfriend Marco.
She's pragmatic: she'd take a **chain job** or take over the garage if the money worked.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, if computers take the inspections and the garage closes before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A simple route into **machinery jobs** without computer courses.
